transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (BrightScale), Samir Patel (BrightScale), Lina Gomez (BrightScale Security), Jonah Kim (BrightScale SRE)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll keep this hands on. I'm Alex from Redwood, with Priya on the se side who'll drive the tuning bits.
[00:12] Marta: thanks alex, we really want to push throughput on our rlhf inference path, low latency still matters but cost is a big factor.
[00:21] Priya: great, quick agenda - continuous batching overview, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, token limits), kv cache behavior on long prefix workloads, quantization options, and then gaps for vpc/on-prem. we'll leave 15 for next steps.
[00:35] Samir: quick context - our typical requests are a 2-4 utterance chat history plus policy prompt, median seq length ~ 140 tokens, tail up to 1024 in open cases. We do ~1.2k reqs/s at peak, currently on a mixed fleet of G4+ and A100s.
[00:55] Priya: ok that token distribution matters a lot for batching. continuous batching in our runtime accumulates requests into open batches until either max_num_seqs or max_tokens_per_batch is hit, then we dispatch. So the two knobs interplay - set max_num_seqs too low you hurt throughput, too high you spike latency.
[01:20] Marta: can you give concrete numbers? like what do you run in production for models in the 30b-70b range?
[01:28] Priya: for a 70b model on A100 we often start with max_num_seqs=16 and max_tokens_per_batch about 8192 - that is a target not a hard cap; the scheduler also respects per-device memory and kv cache. For 30b we go to 32 seqs. But it's workload dependent; your median 140 tokens means effective batch size in tokens = num_seqs * avg_tokens.
[01:52] Samir: we see some weird tail latency spikes when a very long request arrives and evicts the kv cache, is that expected?
[01:58] Priya: yeah so kv cache eviction and prefix caching behavior can cause cpu/gpu transfer spikes. The runtime supports prefix/KV caching so repeated prefixes are served from cache. But if a long seq causes the KV cache to reallocate, you'll see a hiccup. There's a knob kv_cache_reserve_ratio which reserves headroom for growth; defaults are conservative.
[02:20] Lina: can you explain the reserve ratio more simply? our security team worries about memory overcommit on on-prem.
[02:27] Priya: sure, kv_cache_reserve_ratio is basically an extra allocation budget for per-seq kv states when we build batches. On dedicated/on-prem you can lower it if you want predictable memory usage, but you might pay in latency because we can't coalesce as aggressively. For predictable tail behavior set reserve to 0.15-0.2 then calibrate.
[02:47] Jonah: is that the same as the "prealloc kv" setting we've seen in the docs? We have some typos in the doc and saw "prealloc kv" vs "KV cask" in the transcript earlier, heh.
[02:56] Alex: yes prealloc kv is the param exposed in the private deployment config, helps avoid realloacs at runtime. Good to reconcile doc naming.
[03:05] Priya: scheduler knobs - two more important ones: batch_timeout_ms and max_num_seqs. batch_timeout controls how long we wait to fill a batch before dispatch. for low latency you set short timeouts (5-10ms) but that reduces throughput. For batchy workloads set 30-50ms and you get better GPU utilization.
[03:28] Samir: currently we have batch_timeout at 8ms and max_num_seqs 24 on our g4 fleet; utilization is low ~45%. What would you recommend?
[03:37] Priya: ok try increasing batch_timeout to 25ms and drop max_num_seqs to 16 for the g4s - g4s have less memory so smaller seq ceiling reduces spiky OOMs. For A100s you can increase max_num_seqs and batch_timeout to 40ms. We'll run bench to tailor.
[03:56] Marta: how do token limits interact? we have per-request limits to avoid runaway tokens.
[04:02] Priya: we have two levels: scheduler token cap (max_tokens_per_batch) and per-request token limit. If a single request exceeds per-request limit it is always dispatched alone which can kill throughput. So enforce per-request caps at the edge, or use pre-splitting for very long contexts.
[04:23] Samir: any automatic splitting?
[04:26] Priya: not automatic server-side today; recommended pattern is lightweight edge splitter that chunks long contexts and reassembles results. We can help with sample code.
[04:33] Alex: also note continuous batching interacts with function-calling or streaming; streaming tends to reduce batchability because it flushes early.
[04:42] Marta: quantization - we are considering nf4/int8 to cut memory. what's the hit on quality and perf?
[04:49] Priya: nf4 is a great middle ground: 2-4x memory reduction with small quality delta on many models. int8 gives more compress but can require per-layer fallback. Runtime supports mixed-precision paths; we recommend running evals on your prompt set. For throughput: quantized models reduce memory so you can increase max_num_seqs and batch sizes, but attention kernel changes mean per-token latency might be slightly higher on some ops.
[05:18] Samir: do we need a different kernel selection for quantized runs?
[05:22] Priya: runtime auto-selects kernels, but you should pin a quantization profile. We have predefined profiles (nf4-default, int8-safe) in the config. For on-prem you can upload custom quant tables.
[05:36] Lina: security question - if we run Private VPC deployment with prealloc kv, are keys ever swapped to disk? we have strict controls on ephemeral storage.
[05:44] Alex: no swapping to disk for KV cache in our default configuration - it's GPU memory and host pinned memory. For on-prem we provide deployment checklist that enforces ephemeral scratch on tmpfs and strict kernel swap off. We'll send the doc.
[05:58] Marta: curious about routing - can we route small low-latency requests to a dedicated low-latency tier and batchy requests to a high-throughput pool?
[06:06] Priya: yes routing policies are first-class: you can route by latency SLO tag or by model tag. For example route short seqs to a low-batch pool with batch_timeout 5ms and route background batchy jobs to a pool with 50ms. That avoids head-of-line blocking.
[06:23] Samir: our concern is multi-tenant GPUs on-prem; how do you isolate noisy neighbors?
[06:29] Priya: Dedicated pools allow GPU reservation and cgroup-level limits; combined with max_num_seqs per-tenant cap we can limit noisy tenants. On-host we also set per-tenant scheduler quotas.
[06:40] Jonah: is there a recommended starting profile for rpc style inference?
[06:44] Priya: yes we have starter profiles in the docs: rpc-low-latency, rpc-high-throughput. I'll share link. rpc-low-latency: batch_timeout 5-10ms, max_num_seqs 8-16, per-request token limit 256. rpc-high-throughput: batch_timeout 30-50ms, max_num_seqs 32-64, max_tokens_per_batch 16384.
[07:08] Marta: we need to watch for the scenario where a single long request occupies the GPU and blocks many small ones. Any mitigations?
[07:15] Priya: two mitigations: per-request token cap (reject or chunk long requests) and preemptive scheduling where long requests are routed to a separate lane. We also support cooperative preemption in Dedicated mode - a long running generation can be checkpointed and resumed to free the GPU temporarily but that needs orchestration.
[07:36] Samir: cooperative preemption sounds heavy, is it stable?
[07:39] Priya: it's in selective use at customers with dedicated pools; it adds complexity. For most cases routing and caps are sufficient.
[07:47] Alex: quick demo note - we'll share a bench spreadsheet that correlates batch_timeout, max_num_seqs and tokens/sec and tail p95. That should give actionable starting points.
[07:56] Marta: okay show us an example config for our 70b model?
[08:00] Priya: example: pool:a100-70b { max_num_seqs: 16, batch_timeout_ms: 40, max_tokens_per_batch: 8192, kv_cache_reserve_ratio: 0.18, quant_profile: nf4-default, prealloc_kv: true }
[08:18] Samir: and for g4?
[08:20] Priya: pool:g4-70b { max_num_seqs: 8, batch_timeout_ms: 25, max_tokens_per_batch: 4096, kv_cache_reserve_ratio: 0.12, quant_profile: nf4-slim, prealloc_kv: true }
[08:36] Lina: any audit/a11y on these config changes? we need auditable rollout and canary testing for compliance.
[08:43] Alex: Redwood Console supports rollout policies - you can canary config changes to a percent of traffic and we keep config-change audit logs plus per-route latency cost deltas. We'll attach the console docs.
[08:56] Marta: do you have recommended metrics to collect during the bench? we want to reproduce in our perf lab.
[09:01] Priya: yes collect tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU util, memory headroom, kv cache hit ratio, batch fill rate, and number of singleton dispatches (requests that go alone).
[09:12] Samir: singleton dispatches are the killer, we see 18% singletons right now.
[09:16] Priya: aim for <5% singletons to hit good GPU efficiency. That means enforcing edge caps and increasing batch_timeout to allow aggregation.
[09:25] Jonah: question on monitoring - do you emit batch-level traces we can ingest?
[09:28] Alex: yes we emit per-batch telemetry with batch size, token count, comp time, and we provide traces to your observability via OpenTelemetry exporter.
[09:37] Marta: ok let's talk through the bench plan - what are you going to run?
[09:40] Priya: we'll run two profiles: 1) baseline with your current config, 2) tuned with suggested knobs. each run 60 minutes, synthetic traffic shaped to your histogram. gather metrics. We'll also test quantized vs fp16 variants.
[09:55] Samir: what's the expected improvement?
[09:57] Priya: rough ballpark for your workload: +35-60% token/sec with tuned batching+quantization; cost per token drops accordingly, latency p95 may increase a bit but p50 should improve.
[10:10] Marta: any risks to model quality with nf4?
[10:13] Priya: small for generation quality on many assistant-style models. We'll run your eval prompt set and measure rouge/embedding-similarity and human sample checks.
[10:25] Lina: security follow ups: we need SOC2 artifacts and a deployment checklist for our on-prem partner.
[10:30] Alex: I'll attach SOC 2 summary and the private deployment checklist. We also support KMS integrations and HSM for key custody.
[10:40] Samir: a few quick clarifications from the CLI config you showed earlier - is max_num_seqs global or per-device?
[10:46] Priya: it's per-device logical limit; scheduler respects device memory and may distribute batches across devices. In multi-gpu model parallel setups it's per-shard. Docs are a bit fuzzy there we should update them.
[10:58] Marta: noted. Also you mentioned cooperative cache warmup - how long does warmup take?
[11:02] Priya: depends - for repeated prefixes minutes to hours depending on repetition. We support pre-warm APIs where you can push frequent contexts and warm the cache before traffic starts. Useful for scheduled jobs.
[11:15] Alex: ok we're near the end, recap: Priya will run bench with two profiles, share tuning guide and starter configs; Alex will send security and pricing artifacts; Marta to share traces and confirm bench windows.
[11:29] Marta: thanks all, this was super useful.
[11:33] Samir: thanks, we'll get those logs over today.
[11:36] Alex: great, logs and confirmations to the thread. we'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench results review.

Notes:
